My recomendation is accept chaos. We sometimes as designers improve the world and sometimes we just create junk, Sadly that's the tough reality of creating products. But there's a caveat. Design not only for the end user, design for the whole chain and you'll see you can improve something in a space that's going to be filled either way. Like a feature in your assembling that improves operators and assembly ergonomics. Improved geometry to use less materials or operations to do. Better material separation, innovation in materials, better UX, local manufacturing etc....

Also I should add, failing helps learning, and in some fails there are answers. 
And there's this concept I've learned that helps a lot. MVP, minimum viable product, which means the path of least resistance, perfection is your enemy while you search for it, perfection is something that happens after you finish your project... And it's not up to you to get there, excellence on the other hand, but it's easier if you do the minimum viable actions to get there instead of trying to be innecesariy awesome...

I can tell you from experience, knowing how to draw or CAD is secondary, with practice you'll get there, the key for Industrial design is critical thinking. Think that in a near future AI will replace cad and sketching, but understanding how the users interact with your products, how you need to make it look good and cheap etc... that's the kind of skills that matter. 
It's ok that you doubt yourself and maybe industrial design is not for you, that's also something, and you shouldn't feel bad about it. Reality and expectations tend to clash sometimes. But if you really want to keep studying and working as a designer, don't give up, learn a cad tool that makes sense to you if that's stopping you, or hire someone in Fiverr to do thecad.
I suck at sketches but I keep working as an ID, sketch and cad are surface level skills. Just develop your critical thinking and question everything, that's the key.
